short: DMRT proteins are the DM-domain transcription factors, named after Drosophila Doublesex and C. elegans MAB-3, the sexual regulators in which the domain was found. Humans have seven well-studied genes, DMRT1, DMRT2, DMRT3, DMRTA1, DMRTA2, DMRTB1 and DMRTC2, plus DMRTC1 paralogues. The DM domain is not a classical zinc finger: two zinc ions are chelated by an intertwined arrangement of cysteines and histidines that cannot be split into independent fingers, and the module ends in a recognition helix. The proteins bind a pseudopalindromic element built from two ACA/TGT half-sites, canonically ACAWTGTW, as dimers and higher-order oligomers. DMRT1 is required for testis differentiation and sustains it after birth; it is the sex-determining gene in chicken, and the 9p24 region containing it is deleted in human 46,XY sex reversal.
long:
## The factors

The DM domain was identified in Drosophila Doublesex (DSX) and C. elegans MAB-3 and is conserved
across animals. Vertebrates have a small family: the seven human genes usually discussed are
DMRT1, DMRT2, DMRT3, DMRTA1 (DMRT4), DMRTA2 (DMRT5), DMRTB1 (DMRT6) and DMRTC2 (DMRT7), with
additional DMRTC1 paralogues that also have measured binding. Outside the DM domain the proteins
share almost no sequence, so the family is defined by its DNA-binding module and not by any
common architecture. That module is structurally unusual. Rather than the independent zinc
fingers of C2H2 or GATA proteins, the DM domain chelates two zinc ions through an intertwined
set of cysteine and histidine ligands that cannot be separated into discrete fingers, followed by
a C-terminal recognition helix and a basic tail. DMRT proteins do not bind as simple monomers:
the crystal structures of human DMRT1 on DNA show tetrameric, trimeric and dimeric modes on the
same kind of site, and ChIP with exonuclease treatment indicates that several of these modes are
used in cells. Expression is restricted. DMRT1 is essentially gonad-specific (Sertoli cells and
germ cells); DMRT2 acts in somites; DMRT3 is in spinal interneurons and gonad; DMRTA2 is in
developing cortex; DMRTB1 and DMRTC2 are germ-cell proteins.

## The motif

The element is a pseudopalindrome assembled from two trinucleotide half-sites that are reverse
complements of one another, ACA and TGT, separated by one or two variable bases. Written as the
literature usually does, the core is ACAWTGTW; the equivalent forward-strand rendering with the
half-sites in the other order is TGTWACA, and this is what the data consensus here,
AATGTAACAA, represents. The two are the same element, not a disagreement. Information is
concentrated on the two ACA/TGT triplets; the spacer base and the flanks are weakly constrained,
which is why individual database models range from a bare six-base TGTADC to a full 13-base
AATGTATCAATTT. Structurally, the early NMR work on the DSX DM domain described contacts in the
minor groove of an undistorted duplex, whereas the later crystal structures of DMRT1 showed two
adjacent antiparallel recognition helices inserted into a widened major groove making
base-specific contacts; the current picture is major-groove reading with minor-groove
stabilization, and this shift is worth knowing when reading older descriptions. In vitro
selection across six of the seven vertebrate proteins returned sites resembling the DSX site for
all of them, differing only in efficiency and in preference at individual positions. The family
is correspondingly cohesive here (0.86 across 20 motifs) and no paralogue is separable by
sequence. Some DMRT models drift toward pure AT-richness: the Vierstra archetype
AC0092:DMRT/HOXB is an ATATATT-like model shared with HOXB, and its nearest neighbours lie
outside the family, a reminder that AT-rich DM sites and AT-rich homeodomain sites are hard to
tell apart.

## Where it acts

DMRT1 occupancy in mouse testis is largely promoter-proximal and promoter-distal in roughly equal
measure, with thousands of sites, and the strongest targets are genes of the male pathway
(SOX9, PTGDS) and genes that DMRT1 must keep off (FOXL2, and the retinoic-acid-responsive meiotic
initiator STRA8). DMRT1 works with and against other gonadal regulators: it opposes FOXL2 and
ESR1/ESR2 in the ovarian program, and cooperates with SOX9 and SF1/NR5A1 in the testis. DMRT3
acts in the spinal cord in circuits that coordinate limb movement. Because the factors are
tissue-restricted, the genomic distribution of DM sites is much broader than the set that is
ever occupied: in a cell that expresses no DMRT protein, the sequence is inert.

## Biology and disease

Dmrt1-null mice have severely dysgenic testes, and postnatal loss of DMRT1 in Sertoli cells
reprograms them toward granulosa cells with activation of FOXL2 and ESR2, so DMRT1 is needed
continuously, not just at the sex-determining step. In chicken, the Z-linked DMRT1 is the male
sex-determining gene, and knockdown feminizes male gonads. In humans, deletions of distal 9p
that remove DMRT1 cause 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis and sex reversal, and point mutations in
residues that contact DNA have the same effect; common variants near DMRT1 are associated with
testicular germ cell tumor risk. Outside sex determination, a premature stop codon in horse
DMRT3 underlies the ability to perform alternate gaits, and the same mutation modeled in mice
disturbs spinal circuit function.

## Reading a hit

The element is short and AT-rich in its flanks, so chance matches are common and the AT-rich
tails are readily confused with homeodomain and other minor-groove AT binders. A match cannot
be assigned to a paralogue: the seven vertebrate DM proteins select nearly the same sequence in
vitro, and most models in these databases come from HT-SELEX or methyl-HT-SELEX on isolated
domains, which measure intrinsic specificity and cannot distinguish family members. The strongest
interpretive constraint is expression: DM sites are only meaningful in tissues where a DMRT
protein is present, which for DMRT1 means gonad. Note also that the JASPAR mouse Dmrt1 matrix
MA1603.2 (TACAAAGT) is an outlier here, with nearest neighbours outside the family, so a hit
scored against that specific model deserves a second look.
caveats: The informative part of a DM site is two ACA/TGT triplets separated by one or two bases, so an effective width of about seven bases plus AT-rich flanks: chance matches are frequent. All seven vertebrate paralogues select nearly identical sequences in vitro, so a hit identifies the family, never the member, and expression is the only practical discriminator. AT-rich renderings of the site overlap homeodomain space, which is visible in the Vierstra AC0092:DMRT/HOXB archetype. Most models here derive from in vitro selection on isolated DM domains, which supports the sequence preference but says nothing about genomic occupancy. The JASPAR mouse Dmrt1 model MA1603.2 does not match the family consensus.
